Hook: In 2007, three researchers at the University of California, Irvine, set out to answer a simple question about a music player. Apple's fifth-generation iPod, the one with a thirty-gigabyte hard drive, sold in America for 299 dollars. Engraved on the back were two lines: designed by Apple in California, assembled in China. The trade statistics agreed with the label. When an iPod crossed the Pacific, its whole factory value was counted as an import from China. So who made it? The researchers, Greg Linden, Kenneth Kraemer and Jason Dedrick, did something different. They followed the money.

Of the 299 dollars, about 75 went to the shops and the distributors that sold it, and 80 went to Apple. The rest, about 144 dollars, paid for the parts. The most expensive part by far was the hard drive, made by Toshiba of Japan, at 73 dollars. And the final assembly in China, the step the label named? 3 dollars 70. Of that, the assembler, a Taiwanese company called Inventec, kept, by the authors' estimate, about 11 cents.
The label, the trade statistics and the money gave three different answers to the question of who makes the thing. This series is about the third answer.
Industry, Built. Part one: where the money goes. When you pay for something, who gets the money, and why them? We will answer it for the object most of us touch first thing every morning: the phone.

Every part of this series puts the same five questions to an industry. What is sold? How is it made, and what does one more cost? Where does the customer's dollar go? Why does the money stay where it does? And what moves it? In this first part we ask them of a single phone, follow its price to the companies that make it, and check each number against what those companies report. One thing before we start: every figure on screen carries its source and the date it describes, because the phone business changed a great deal this year.
